modules.title: Drug Classes, Names & Pharmacology Basics
modules.desc: Generic/brand naming, drug stems, major therapeutic classes, and how drugs work.

lessons.title: Generic vs Brand Names & Drug Stems
lessons.intro: Every drug has one official generic (nonproprietary) name and one or more brand (trade/proprietary) names. The PTCE heavily tests generic↔brand pairs. Learning suffix "stems" lets you identify a drug's class instantly.
bullets: Generic names are lowercase; brand names are capitalized (e.g., lisinopril vs Zestril).

Common stems reveal the class: -pril = ACE inhibitor, -sartan = ARB, -olol = beta blocker, -vastatin = HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor (nystatin is an antifungal for oral candidiasis, not a statin), -prazole = PPI (aripiprazole is an antipsychotic, not a PPI), -tidine = H2 blocker, -azepam/-azolam = benzodiazepine.
-sartan: losartan (Cozaar), valsartan (Diovan). -vastatin: atorvastatin (Lipitor), simvastatin (Zocor), rosuvastatin (Crestor).

Antibiotics: -cillin = penicillins (amoxicillin), ceph- = cephalosporins (cephalexin/Keflex), -thromycin = macrolides (azithromycin/Zithromax, clarithromycin; -mycin is not one class — vancomycin is a glycopeptide), -floxacin = fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin/Cipro).
On the exam, brand names often appear in the question and you must supply the generic class or a clinical fact.
keyPoints: One generic name, many brand names
Learn stems to identify the class

lessons.title: Cardiovascular & Cholesterol Agents
lessons.intro: The largest PTCE medication group. Know the class, brand name, and key safety point for each.
bullets: ACE inhibitors (-pril): lisinopril (Zestril/Prinivil), enalapril — for HTN/HF; classic dry cough (bradykinin) and angioedema risk.
ARBs (-sartan): losartan, valsartan — same indications as ACEIs without the cough; both classes are teratogenic (avoid in pregnancy).
Beta blockers (-olol): metoprolol (Lopressor=IR tartrate, Toprol-XL=ER succinate), atenolol (Tenormin) — lower HR/BP; caution in asthma, do not stop abruptly.
Calcium channel blockers: amlodipine (Norvasc, dihydropyridine → vasodilation, ankle edema); diltiazem/verapamil (non-DHP → also slow heart rate).
Statins (-vastatin): atorvastatin, simvastatin, rosuvastatin — lower LDL; report unexplained muscle pain (myopathy/rhabdomyolysis); simvastatin interacts with grapefruit (CYP3A4).
Diuretics: hydrochlorothiazide/HCTZ (thiazide, hypokalemia), furosemide/Lasix (loop, "loses potassium"), spironolactone (potassium-sparing).

Clopidogrel (Plavix) is a thienopyridine P2Y12 platelet inhibitor. Tablets contain 75 mg clopidogrel. It is indicated to reduce MI and stroke in acute coronary syndrome, and in recent MI, recent stroke, or established peripheral arterial disease.

lessons.title: Antibiotics & Anti-Infectives
lessons.intro: Know the major antibiotic classes, their stems, spectrum, and signature safety points.
bullets: Penicillins (-cillin): amoxicillin, amoxicillin/clavulanate (Augmentin) — common for ear/strep; watch for allergy/anaphylaxis.

Amoxicillin: there are reports of severe reactions to cephalosporins in people with a history of penicillin hypersensitivity. Before amoxicillin, ask about prior reactions to penicillins, cephalosporins, or other allergens.
Cephalosporins (ceph-/-cef-): cephalexin (Keflex). Generations 1–5 are not steadily broader gram-negative coverage; ceftaroline covers MRSA (gram-positive) plus some gram-negatives.
Macrolides (-thromycin): azithromycin (Zithromax/Z-Pak = 6 tabs, 500 mg day 1 then 250 mg ×4), clarithromycin — QT prolongation risk.

Fluoroquinolones (-floxacin): ciprofloxacin (Cipro), levofloxacin — BOXED WARNING: tendinitis and tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, CNS effects, and myasthenia gravis exacerbation. Reserve them when there is no alternative for acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis, uncomplicated cystitis, and acute sinusitis. Age >60 raises tendon-rupture risk. QT prolongation is a separate warning, not the box. Not first choice in children (arthropathy); approved for some pediatric uses (anthrax, plague).
Tetracyclines: doxycycline, tetracycline — avoid in children <8 and pregnancy (permanent tooth discoloration); chelate with dairy/antacids.
Sulfonamides: sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim (Bactrim) — sulfa allergy, hyperkalemia, photosensitivity.
Sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim (Bactrim): fatalities and serious reactions include severe cutaneous adverse reactions, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis.
Antifungals: fluconazole (Diflucan). Antivirals: acyclovir (Zovirax), oseltamivir (Tamiflu).
Oral acyclovir is indicated for acute herpes zoster (shingles), for initial and recurrent genital herpes, and for chickenpox (varicella).

Oseltamivir (Tamiflu) is an influenza neuraminidase inhibitor for treatment of acute, uncomplicated influenza A and B in patients 2 weeks of age and older who have been symptomatic for no more than 48 hours, and for prophylaxis of influenza A and B in patients 1 year and older.
Fluconazole (Diflucan) is indicated for vaginal candidiasis, oropharyngeal and esophageal candidiasis, and cryptococcal meningitis.
Oseltamivir (Tamiflu) treatment, adults and adolescents 13 years and older: 75 mg twice daily for 5 days.
keyPoints: FQ box: tendon, neuropathy, CNS, myasthenia

lessons.title: Endocrine: Diabetes & Thyroid
lessons.intro: Diabetes agents are frequently tested by class and mechanism; thyroid drugs have strict administration rules.
bullets: Metformin (Glucophage): first-line biguanide for T2DM; GI upset; take with food. Hold at the time of or before iodinated contrast only if eGFR is 30–60, or there is a history of liver disease, alcoholism, or heart failure, or the contrast is intra-arterial; recheck eGFR at 48 hours and restart if stable (lactic acidosis risk).
Sulfonylureas: glipizide, glimepiride, glyburide — stimulate insulin release; main risk is HYPOGLYCEMIA.
SGLT2 inhibitors (-gliflozin): empagliflozin (Jardiance) — increase urinary glucose excretion; genital infections, DKA risk.
GLP-1 agonists: semaglutide (Ozempic), liraglutide (Victoza) — injectable, weight loss, GI upset.

Semaglutide (Ozempic) BOXED WARNING: risk of thyroid C-cell tumors. In rodents, semaglutide causes thyroid C-cell tumors. It is unknown whether Ozempic causes thyroid C-cell tumors, including medullary thyroid carcinoma (MTC), in humans. Contraindicated with a personal or family history of MTC or with Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia syndrome type 2 (MEN 2).

Liraglutide (Victoza) BOXED WARNING: risk of thyroid C-cell tumors. In rats and mice, liraglutide causes thyroid C-cell tumors. It is unknown whether Victoza causes thyroid C-cell tumors, including MTC, in humans. Contraindicated with a personal or family history of MTC and in MEN 2.
Semaglutide (Ozempic) is injected subcutaneously once weekly. Start at 0.25 mg once weekly. After 4 weeks, increase to 0.5 mg once weekly. A missed dose may be given within 5 days.
DPP-4 inhibitors (-gliptin): sitagliptin (Januvia). Thiazolidinediones (-glitazone): pioglitazone (Actos) — weight gain, fluid retention/HF caution.

Insulin types: rapid (lispro/Humalog, aspart/NovoLog ~15 min), short (Regular), intermediate (NPH), long (glargine/Lantus — about 24 h, no pronounced peak; degludec/Tresiba — at least 42 h). Detemir (Levemir) is discontinued in the US. Refrigerate unopened; in-use time is product-specific (Lantus vial: 28 days, refrigerated or room temperature; Lantus SoloStar: 28 days at room temperature only, do not refrigerate); never freeze.
Levothyroxine (Synthroid): T4 replacement — take on empty stomach 30–60 min before breakfast, separate from calcium/iron by 4 h, consistent brand.
keyPoints: Metformin contrast hold is only for higher-risk patients
Insulin onset: rapid 15min, glargine no peak
Ozempic box: thyroid C-cell tumors; no MTC or MEN 2

lessons.title: CNS, Psychiatric & Pain Agents
lessons.intro: Antidepressants, anxiolytics, sedatives, and analgesics — know class, schedule, and key warnings.
bullets: SSRIs (no single class suffix; examples: fluoxetine (Prozac), sertraline (Zoloft), escitalopram (Lexapro)) — take 2–4 weeks to work; risk serotonin syndrome with MAOIs/triptans. -oxetine is not SSRI-only (duloxetine is an SNRI).

Lamotrigine ER (Lamictal XR) BOXED WARNING: serious rashes, including Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Incidence of these rashes is approximately 0.8% (8 per 1,000) in pediatric patients aged 2 to 16 years on adjunctive immediate-release lamotrigine for epilepsy, and 0.3% (3 per 1,000) in adults on adjunctive therapy for epilepsy. Rare toxic epidermal necrolysis and rash-related death are reported. Lamictal XR is not approved under age 13.
SNRIs: duloxetine (Cymbalta) — depression, anxiety, neuropathic pain; venlafaxine (Effexor XR) — MDD, GAD, social anxiety, and panic, not neuropathic pain.
Benzodiazepines (-azepam/-azolam): alprazolam (Xanax), lorazepam (Ativan), diazepam (Valium) — C-IV, sedation/dependence; overdose reversed by flumazenil.
Z-hypnotics for insomnia: zolpidem (Ambien), eszopiclone (Lunesta) — C-IV; next-day impairment.
NSAIDs: ibuprofen (Advil/Motrin), naproxen (Aleve), meloxicam (Mobic), celecoxib (Celebrex) — GI bleed/CV risk, take with food.
Acetaminophen (Tylenol): max 4 g/day (many recommend 3 g); hepatotoxicity in overdose; antidote N-acetylcysteine. Often combined with opioids (Norco = hydrocodone/APAP).
Do not use acetaminophen with any other prescription or nonprescription drug that contains acetaminophen.
Opioids (C-II): oxycodone, hydrocodone/APAP (Norco), tramadol (C-IV) — sedation, constipation (no tolerance), respiratory depression; reversed by naloxone.

Methylphenidate ER (Concerta) is a CNS stimulant for ADHD in patients 6 to 65 years old. BOXED WARNING: high potential for abuse and misuse, which can lead to a substance use disorder, including addiction. Misuse and abuse can result in overdose and death.
Sumatriptan tablets (Imitrex) are a 5-HT1B/1D agonist (triptan) for acute migraine with or without aura in adults. Not for prevention of migraine. Tablets contain 25 mg, 50 mg, or 100 mg sumatriptan.

Aripiprazole (Abilify) is an atypical antipsychotic indicated for schizophrenia. BOXED WARNING: increased mortality in elderly patients with dementia-related psychosis. Not approved for dementia-related psychosis.

lessons.title: Respiratory, GI & Miscellaneous
lessons.intro: Respiratory inhalers, GI acid agents, and other high-frequency drugs.
bullets: SABA rescue inhalers: albuterol (ProAir RespiClick, Ventolin HFA) — short-acting beta-agonist. Ventolin HFA: prime before first use. ProAir RespiClick: does not require priming.
Inhaled corticosteroids (maintenance): fluticasone (Flovent); LABA: salmeterol (never used alone in asthma).
Montelukast (Singulair): leukotriene receptor antagonist for asthma/allergic rhinitis — boxed warning for neuropsychiatric effects.

PPIs (-prazole; aripiprazole is not a PPI): omeprazole (Prilosec), pantoprazole (Protonix), esomeprazole (Nexium) — take 30–60 min before the first meal; long-term use → B12 deficiency, fracture risk.
H2 blockers (-tidine): famotidine (Pepcid) — reduce gastric acid; weaker than PPIs.
Bisphosphonates: alendronate (Fosamax) for osteoporosis — take with plain water 30+ min before food and remain upright to prevent esophagitis.

Alendronate (Fosamax) treatment of osteoporosis in postmenopausal women and in men: 10 mg daily or 70 mg once weekly. Prevention of osteoporosis in postmenopausal women: 5 mg daily or 35 mg once weekly.
Gout: allopurinol (Zyloprim, chronic prevention), colchicine (acute flare). Antihistamines: loratadine (Claritin, non-sedating), diphenhydramine (Benadryl, sedating).

Allopurinol: serious and sometimes fatal dermatologic reactions, including toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) and Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), in approximately 5 in 10,000 (0.05%) patients. Discontinue at the first appearance of skin rash.
Tamsulosin is an alpha-1A adrenoceptor antagonist for the signs and symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia. It is not indicated for hypertension.
Prednisone is a glucocorticoid (systemic corticosteroid). Oral tablets contain 5 mg, 10 mg, or 20 mg. One labeled use is adjunctive short-term therapy in rheumatoid arthritis.
Tri-Sprintec (norgestimate and ethinyl estradiol) is a combination oral contraceptive indicated to prevent pregnancy in females of reproductive potential.
Tri-Sprintec BOXED WARNING: cigarette smoking increases the risk of serious cardiovascular events from combination oral contraceptives. Contraindicated in women over 35 years of age who smoke.
keyPoints: Albuterol = rescue; prime Ventolin HFA, not ProAir RespiClick
Alendronate treatment: 10 mg daily or 70 mg weekly

modules.title: High-Alert, LASA & Special-Population Medications
modules.desc: High-alert drugs, look-alike/sound-alike pairs, monitoring-intensive agents (former dedicated NTI list), and pregnancy/teratogen rules.

lessons.title: High-Alert Medications
lessons.intro: High-alert medications bear a heightened risk of significant harm when used in error. The ISMP list is a PTCE favorite.
bullets: High-alert classes: insulin, anticoagulants (warfarin, heparin, DOACs), opioids, concentrated electrolytes (KCl), chemotherapy, and methotrexate.
Methotrexate tablets (Trexall) for rheumatoid arthritis: recommended starting dosage 7.5 mg orally once weekly. BOXED WARNING: tablets inadvertently administered once daily have resulted in death.
Insulin: wrong-dose errors are common and dangerous; U-100 = 100 units/mL; use independent double checks.
Anticoagulants: warfarin (monitor INR), heparin (monitor aPTT, HIT risk), DOACs (apixaban/Eliquis, rivaroxaban/Xarelto) — bleeding is the major harm.

Warfarin is a vitamin K antagonist indicated for prophylaxis and treatment of venous thrombosis and pulmonary embolism; prophylaxis and treatment of thromboembolic complications associated with atrial fibrillation and/or cardiac valve replacement; and reduction in the risk of death, recurrent MI, and thromboembolic events such as stroke after myocardial infarction.

Apixaban (Eliquis) is a factor Xa inhibitor indicated to reduce the risk of stroke and systemic embolism in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, for DVT prophylaxis after hip or knee replacement, and for treatment of DVT and PE and reduction of recurrent DVT and PE.

Rivaroxaban (Xarelto) is a factor Xa inhibitor indicated to reduce the risk of stroke and systemic embolism in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation, for treatment of DVT, for treatment of PE, for reduction in the risk of recurrence of DVT or PE, and for DVT prophylaxis, which may lead to PE, after knee or hip replacement.
Concentrated potassium chloride injection must ALWAYS be diluted before IV use — undiluted rapid IV push can cause fatal cardiac arrest.
Risk-reduction strategies: independent double checks, standardized order sets, Tall Man lettering, and pharmacist profile review before ADC removal.
keyPoints: Insulin, anticoagulants, opioids, KCl, chemo = high-alert
Oral methotrexate for RA: once weekly

lessons.title: Look-Alike Sound-Alike (LASA) & Tall Man Lettering
lessons.intro: LASA pairs cause many dispensing errors. ISMP recommends Tall Man lettering to differentiate them.
bullets: Tall Man lettering capitalizes the DISsimilar letters: predniSONE vs prednisoLONE; hydrALAZINE vs hydrOXYzine; DOBUTamine vs DOPamine; niCARdipine vs NIFEdipine.
Classic LASA pairs: predniSONE/prednisoLONE, hydrALAZINE (BP)/hydrOXYzine (antihistamine), clonidine/clonazepam, lamotrigine/lamivudine.
Prevention: segregate look-alike products on shelves, add warning labels to bins, use barcode scanning at verification, and read the full name + indication.
The goal is to draw attention to the differing letters, not to change pronunciation.

lessons.title: Narrow Therapeutic Index & Monitoring (optional archive)
lessons.intro: OPTIONAL / NOT EMPHASIZED ON THE 2026 PTCE. A dedicated NTI-list knowledge area (old 1.8) was removed from the January 2026 outline. Skip this lesson on the default path. These agents still matter as high-alert / monitoring drugs if you want extra review.
bullets: Digoxin (Lanoxin): cardiac glycoside for HF/AFib — toxicity shows nausea, vomiting, and yellow-green visual halos; check level and potassium.
Warfarin: monitor INR; keep dietary vitamin K intake consistent.
Lithium, phenytoin (Dilantin), theophylline, and carbamazepine are other classic NTI drugs requiring levels.
Hypokalemia (low K+) increases digoxin toxicity risk — diuretics that waste potassium compound this.

lessons.title: Pregnancy, Teratogens & Special Populations
lessons.intro: Certain drugs are contraindicated in pregnancy; technicians must recognize teratogens and handling restrictions.
bullets: Known teratogens (avoid in pregnancy): isotretinoin (Accutane), warfarin, methotrexate, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, tetracyclines, valproate, and finasteride. Statins are not an absolute avoid: stop them in most pregnant patients and weigh the individual need.
Isotretinoin requires the iPLEDGE REMS program with strict pregnancy-prevention measures.

Finasteride: pregnant women should not handle crushed or broken tablets (skin absorption). Dutasteride (Avodart) is a capsule; pregnant women should not handle the capsules because dutasteride can be absorbed through the skin from leakage.
Pediatric caution: tetracyclines (<8 y tooth staining), fluoroquinolones (cartilage), aspirin in children with viral illness (Reye's syndrome).
The old letter categories (A/B/C/D/X) were replaced by the Pregnancy and Lactation Labeling Rule (PLLR) narrative format, but "Category X = teratogen" still appears on older references/exams.

modules.title: Dosage Forms, Routes, Storage & Interactions
modules.desc: Dosage-form handling rules, routes of administration, storage requirements, and major interactions.

lessons.title: Dosage Forms & Routes
lessons.intro: How a drug is formulated determines how it must be handled and administered — a frequent PTCE topic.
bullets: Sublingual (SL) dissolves under the tongue for rapid absorption and bypasses first-pass metabolism (nitroglycerin). Buccal = between cheek and gum.
Enteric-coated (EC) resists stomach acid and dissolves in the small intestine — do NOT crush (aspirin EC, omeprazole).
Extended-release (ER/XL/SR/CR/LA) releases over time — do NOT crush or chew (risk of dose dumping). TOPROL-XL is scored and may be split; do not crush or chew it.
Orally disintegrating tablets (ODT) dissolve on the tongue; effervescent tablets must be fully dissolved in water first.
Transdermal patches give steady absorption and bypass first-pass; rotate sites, never cut reservoir patches, fold before disposal (fentanyl patch is high-alert).

Suspensions: "shake well before use." Many nasal sprays and metered-dose inhalers such as Ventolin HFA require priming before first use or after prolonged non-use. ProAir RespiClick does not require priming.
keyPoints: Do NOT crush or chew EC or ER; Toprol-XL may be split
Prime Ventolin HFA; do not prime ProAir RespiClick

lessons.title: Storage Requirements
lessons.intro: Proper storage preserves potency and safety; the PTCE tests specific temperature requirements.
bullets: Refrigerated (36–46°F / 2–8°C): unopened insulin, many vaccines, some biologics. Reconstituted antibiotic suspensions are not all refrigerated.

Unopened insulin must be refrigerated; once in use, time is product-specific (Lantus vial: 28 days, refrigerated or room temperature; Lantus SoloStar: 28 days at room temperature only, do not refrigerate; Tresiba: 56 days). Never freeze insulin. Detemir (Levemir) is discontinued in the US.
Amoxicillin suspension: discard unused portion after 14 days. Refrigeration is preferable, not required. Azithromycin oral suspension: store at 5–30°C (41–86°F) and use within 10 days.
Room temperature (68–77°F / 20–25°C) is the default for most tablets/capsules; protect from moisture and light.
Nitroglycerin SL tablets: keep in the original glass container, tightly capped after each use, at room temperature, to prevent loss of potency.
Most refrigerated vaccines must be stored at 2–8°C (36–46°F) and must NOT be frozen; some require frozen or ultra-cold storage.

Once a multi-dose vial is opened (needle-punctured), date it and discard it within 28 days unless the manufacturer states another date for that opened vial. The beyond-use date should never exceed the manufacturer's original expiration date.
Access to areas where hazardous drugs are handled must be restricted to authorized personnel. Designated areas must include storage of hazardous drugs.

A multi-dose vial used for more than one patient is kept and accessed in a clean medication preparation area, away from immediate patient treatment areas. If it enters a treatment area, dedicate it to that one patient.
keyPoints: Unopened insulin 2–8°C; SoloStar in use is room temp only
Amox susp: 14 days, fridge preferable not required; azithromycin susp: 5–30°C, 10 days
Opened multi-dose vial: 28 days unless the label says otherwise

lessons.title: Major Drug Interactions
lessons.intro: Technicians flag potential interactions for the pharmacist. Know the classic high-yield combinations.
bullets: Therapeutic duplication: two or more drugs from the same therapeutic class when the combined daily dose risks an adverse medical result. Flag it for the pharmacist.
Warfarin + NSAIDs/aspirin → increased bleeding risk; warfarin + many antibiotics (Bactrim, metronidazole, macrolides) → increased INR.
Warfarin: eat a normal diet and keep vitamin K intake consistent. Avoid drastic changes such as large amounts of leafy green vegetables.
MAOI + SSRI/serotonergic drugs → serotonin syndrome (avoid; require washout period).
Sildenafil (Viagra) + nitrates (nitroglycerin) → severe hypotension (contraindicated).
Grapefruit juice inhibits intestinal CYP3A4 → raises levels of simvastatin and many other 3A4 substrates.
St. John's wort, a dietary supplement, is a strong CYP3A inducer. The effect varies widely and is preparation dependent.

Products containing St. John's wort may decrease the effectiveness of combined oral contraceptives such as Tri-Sprintec. Use back-up contraception during the enzyme inducer and for 28 days after it is stopped.
Biotin, often found in dietary supplements, can significantly interfere with certain lab tests and cause incorrect results that may go undetected, including falsely low troponin.
ACE inhibitor + potassium-sparing diuretic (spironolactone) or K+ supplements → hyperkalemia.
Calcium/iron/antacids chelate and block absorption of tetracyclines, fluoroquinolones, and levothyroxine — separate administration by several hours.
keyPoints: St. John's wort = strong CYP3A inducer
Biotin can falsify some lab tests

modules.title: Error Prevention, Reporting & Continuous Quality Improvement
modules.desc: The medication-use process, error categories, reporting programs, and quality-improvement methods.

lessons.title: The Medication-Use Process & the Five Rights
lessons.intro: Medication safety is built on verifying the "five rights" at every step and understanding where errors occur.
bullets: The five rights: right PATIENT, right DRUG, right DOSE, right ROUTE, right TIME. (Some add right documentation and right indication.)
The medication-use process: prescribing → transcribing/order entry → dispensing → administration → monitoring. Errors can occur at each step.
A technician's role: accurate order entry, correct product selection, barcode scanning, and flagging concerns to the pharmacist.
Verify the patient with two identifiers (full name + date of birth) before filling or dispensing.

lessons.title: Error Types, Near Misses & NCC MERP Categories
lessons.intro: Know error severity, the prescription error types on outline 3.5, and the ISMP abbreviations that cause them.
bullets: A near miss (close call) is an error INTERCEPTED before reaching the patient — report it to fix system weaknesses.
NCC MERP category A = circumstances with error potential.
Category B = error did NOT reach patient.
Category C = reached patient, NO harm.
Category D = reached the patient and required monitoring to confirm no harm and/or intervention to preclude harm.
Categories E–I = increasing harm.
Category E = temporary harm requiring intervention.
Category F = hospitalization.
Category G = permanent harm.
Category H = life-sustaining intervention.
Category I = death.
Outline 3.5 examples: incorrect dose, quantity, patient, drug, and route.
Wrong time and omission are other error types; they are not the outline examples.
Incorrect drug dosage on prospective DUR: daily dosage = strength × quantity dispensed ÷ days' supply.
If that daily dosage lies outside the predetermined standard, stop and notify the pharmacist.
ISMP Do Not Use minimum list: spell out units (never U).
Spell out international units (never IU).
Write daily or every other day (never QD or QOD).
Write morphine sulfate or magnesium sulfate (never MS, MSO4, or MgSO4).
Use a leading zero (0.5 mg, not .5 mg).
Do not use a trailing zero (1 mg, not 1.0 mg).
Also on the ISMP error-prone list, but not that minimum Do Not Use set: write mL (never cc); write mcg (never µg).
Eye and ear abbreviations are error-prone: do not use OD, OS, OU, AD, AS, or AU; write right eye, left eye, both eyes, right ear, left ear, or both ears.
More ISMP error-prone abbreviations: write discharge or discontinue (D/C meant as discharge has been read as discontinued).
Write half-strength or bedtime (HS/hs swap those meanings).
Write subcut or subcutaneously (SC, SQ, sub q).
Write 3 times weekly (TIW has been read as 3 times a day).
keyPoints: Leading zero on; trailing zero off
mL not cc; mcg not µg; spell eye/ear

lessons.title: Reporting Programs & Recalls
lessons.intro: Know where and how medication errors and adverse events are reported, and the FDA recall classes.
bullets: FDA MedWatch: voluntary reporting of adverse events, product problems, and medication errors (Form 3500 for professionals, 3500B for consumers).
Product integrity: report a product-quality concern to MedWatch when quality, authenticity, performance, or safety is in doubt.
Examples: suspect counterfeit, contamination, defective components, poor packaging or product mix-up, questionable stability, labeling concerns.
ISMP MERP (Medication Errors Reporting Program): voluntary, CONFIDENTIAL national error reporting to share prevention strategies.
VAERS: Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (for vaccines).
Anyone may report to VAERS.
Healthcare providers are required to report an adverse event on the VAERS Table of Reportable Events Following Vaccination that occurs within the specified time.
Healthcare providers are required to report an adverse event the manufacturer lists as a contraindication to further doses.
Recall Class I = reasonable probability of serious adverse health consequences or death.
Recall Class II = temporary or medically reversible harm, or a remote probability of serious harm.
Recall Class III = adverse health consequences not likely.
When a recall occurs: check lot numbers, quarantine affected stock, and follow the recall instructions for return/disposal.
keyPoints: Class I = serious consequences or death

lessons.title: Continuous Quality Improvement (CQI)
lessons.intro: Quality improvement uses structured methods to reduce errors and improve processes.
bullets: Root cause analysis (RCA): a SYSTEMS-based review after an error to find underlying process failures — not individual blame.
PDSA cycle (Plan-Do-Study-Act): the standard iterative cycle for testing and refining quality-improvement changes.
Independent double checks: two qualified staff separately verify high-alert medications (insulin, anticoagulants, chemotherapy) before dispensing/administration.
Also on the ISMP acute-care high-alert list: neuromuscular blocking agents (succinylcholine, rocuronium, vecuronium) and oral sulfonylureas (glimepiride, glipiZIDE, glyBURIDE).
Insulin U-500 and oral methotrexate for nononcologic use are singled out for special emphasis.
ISMP community/ambulatory high-alert categories also include oral and parenteral immunosuppressants (azaTHIOprine, cycloSPORINE, tacrolimus).
Pediatric liquid medications that require measurement are also on that community/ambulatory high-alert list.
Humulin R U-500 is 500 units/mL, 5 times as much insulin in 1 mL as U-100 (100 units/mL).
Use only a U-500 insulin syringe with the vial. A U-100 syringe used for a U-500 dose can give a 5-times overdose.
Do not mix it with any other insulin and do not inject it intravenously.

Prospective DUR, before the prescription is filled or delivered (at order entry), screens for therapeutic duplication, drug-disease contraindication, drug-drug interaction, incorrect drug dosage, incorrect duration of treatment, drug-allergy interaction, and clinical abuse/misuse.
Retrospective DUR reviews patterns afterward.
Part D concurrent DUR is the review of prescribed therapy before each prescription is dispensed, typically at the point of sale or point of distribution.

It includes age/gender-related contraindications, overutilization and underutilization, drug-drug interactions, incorrect dosage or duration, drug-allergy contraindications, and clinical abuse/misuse.
Medication reconciliation compares all home medications to new orders at EVERY transition of care (admission, transfer, discharge).
keyPoints: Med rec at every transition of care

modules.title: USP Chapter IDs, Hazardous Drugs & Infection Control
modules.desc: Recognize which USP chapter applies, handle hazardous drugs, and meet 3.6 hygiene and counting-tray cleaning standards. Sterile cleanroom depth and dedicated USP <795> technique are optional/archive — not core 2026 PTCE.

lessons.title: USP Standards Overview
lessons.intro: Know which USP chapter applies. Dedicated nonsterile compounding procedures (old 1.9 / 4.1) were removed from the January 2026 outline — do not treat <795> technique or BUD tables as core tested skills.
bullets: USP <795>: NONSTERILE compounding chapter (oral suspensions, topicals, capsules). Removed as a dedicated 2026 procedure skill — chapter ID only.
USP <797>: STERILE compounding chapter (IV admixtures, injections, ophthalmics). Cleanroom procedure and garbing depth are optional archive, not core PTCE.
USP <800>: safe HANDLING of HAZARDOUS DRUGS across both sterile and nonsterile settings — PPE, containment (C-PEC/C-SEC), and personnel protection.
Beyond-use date (BUD): the date after which a COMPOUNDED preparation must NOT be used — assigned per USP limits and stability data, NOT the manufacturer expiration date.

lessons.title: Sterile Compounding: Cleanroom & Garbing (optional archive)
lessons.intro: OPTIONAL / NOT EMPHASIZED ON THE 2026 PTCE. Sterile cleanroom design and garbing are CSPT-level skills, not core PTCE content. Do not treat cleanroom categories or risk levels as required exam material.
bullets: Optional enrichment only: ISO 5 = compounding area (PEC/hood), ISO 7 = buffer room, ISO 8 = ante-room. These classes are not a required PTCE category list.
Laminar airflow workbenches provide ISO 5 HEPA-filtered air; work at least 6 inches inside the hood and avoid blocking first air.
If you review garbing, the order is DIRTIEST to CLEANEST: shoe covers → hair/beard cover → face mask → hand hygiene → gown → sterile gloves LAST.
Hand hygiene: scrub hands and forearms before the gown; don sterile powder-free gloves last; sanitize gloves with sterile 70% IPA.
Clean the PEC with sterile 70% isopropyl alcohol; buffer/ante rooms are cleaned per a defined schedule.
keyPoints: Shoes, hair, mask, hands, gown, gloves

lessons.title: Hazardous Drugs & Infection Control
lessons.intro: Safe handling protects both patients and workers from hazardous-drug exposure and contamination.
bullets: NIOSH maintains the list of hazardous drugs (antineoplastics, hormones, some antivirals).
Hazardous-drug compounding PPE: TWO pairs of chemotherapy-tested gloves + an impermeable gown; add eye/face and respiratory protection per risk.
Use a containment primary engineering control (C-PEC, e.g., BSC or CACI) inside a containment secondary engineering control (C-SEC) with negative pressure for HDs.
Hand hygiene: soap and water for at least 20 seconds when hands are visibly soiled, and during care of patients with suspected or confirmed infection during outbreaks of C. difficile and norovirus.
Unless hands are visibly soiled, an alcohol-based rub (hand sanitizer) is preferred in most clinical situations.

CDC infection-control PPE when using gown, mask or respirator, goggles or face shield, and gloves: don gown, then mask or respirator, then goggles or face shield, then gloves extended over the gown cuff.
Remove gloves, then goggles or face shield, then gown, then mask or respirator.
Counting trays and countertops (outline 3.6): wipe with 70% isopropyl alcohol between fills.
Clean again after penicillin, sulfa, or a hazardous drug before the next prescription.
Use a dedicated tray for hazardous drugs.
Sharps (needles/syringes): rigid, puncture-resistant, closable sharps containers — never regular trash or recycling; never recap by hand.
Vaccine storage: most refrigerated at 2–8°C (36–46°F), do NOT freeze; monitor with calibrated thermometers and document temperatures.
keyPoints: 70% IPA between fills; dedicated HD tray

lessons.title: USP <795> nonsterile technique (optional archive)
lessons.intro: OPTIONAL / NOT EMPHASIZED ON THE 2026 PTCE. Dedicated nonsterile compounding procedures (old 1.9 / related 4.1) were removed. Keep this only as historical review. Default-path study is chapter ID, hazardous-drug handling, and counting-tray/counter hygiene.
bullets: Historical <795> technique topics included BUD assignment by risk, component selection, and nonsterile compounding steps (trituration, geometric dilution, levigation).
Those procedure skills, including nonsterile BUD tables, are not a January 2026 tested knowledge area — do not memorize them on the default path.
If you see a BUD/technique item, treat it as archive — not core PTCE.
Still in scope nearby: which chapter is <795> vs <797> vs <800>, and 3.6 cleaning of trays, counters, equipment, handwashing, and PPE.

modules.title: Safety Technologies, Workflow & Pharmacist Intervention
modules.desc: Barcode/ADC safeguards, REMS hand-off, pharmacist-intervention triggers (DUR, OTC, substitution), and immunization workflow (VIS before the dose, post-immunization care, VAERS).

lessons.title: Safety Technology & Workflow Safeguards
lessons.intro: Technology and process design reduce dispensing errors at the point of care.
bullets: Barcode scanning verifies the correct product (NDC) against the order at the point of verification, reducing wrong-drug errors.
Automated dispensing cabinets (ADCs): requiring pharmacist PROFILE REVIEW before a drug can be removed closes the dangerous "override" gap.
Drug utilization review (DUR): prospective screening at order entry; technicians flag interaction/duplication alerts to the pharmacist for the clinical decision.
Auxiliary (warning) labels communicate cautions: "May cause drowsiness," "Take with food," "Avoid alcohol," "Refrigerate."
REMS (Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy): FDA-required programs for known serious risks.
Current examples include iPLEDGE (isotretinoin) and THALOMID/lenalidomide.
TIRF is not a routine current enroll-and-dispense REMS: production stopped September 30, 2024, and the REMS accepts no new enrollments.
The Clozapine REMS was removed effective June 13, 2025 — do not treat clozapine as a pharmacy REMS.
Tall Man lettering, look-alike bin segregation, and limiting available concentrations/strengths are additional error-reduction strategies.
FDA tall-man pair: buPROPion vs busPIRone.
Issues that require pharmacist intervention (outline 3.3): DUR alerts, adverse drug events, OTC recommendations, therapeutic substitution, misuse/adherence concerns, allergies, and drug interactions.
Overutilization means quantity, strength, or duration greater than necessary to reach the therapeutic goal, or enough to risk a clinically significant undesirable effect, or both.
Underutilization means insufficient quantity, strength, or duration to reach the therapeutic goal, or enough to risk a clinically significant undesirable effect, or both.
Flag both to the pharmacist.
An adverse event is any untoward medical occurrence associated with the use of a drug product in humans, whether or not it is considered related to the drug.
A medication error may or may not be associated with an adverse event.
Off-label use, misuse, and abuse inconsistent with the FDA-approved labeling are not medication errors.
A technician's job at those alerts is to stop, gather the facts, and notify the pharmacist — not to override a clinical alert or recommend a product.
keyPoints: iPLEDGE, THALOMID; not clozapine or new TIRF

lessons.title: Pharmacist Intervention & Immunization Workflow (VIS / VAERS)
lessons.intro: Outline 3.3 and 3.4 include pharmacist intervention and event reporting. Immunizing pharmacies add VIS (before the dose), post-immunization observation, and VAERS. Purple Book biologics interchangeability is not a 2026 PTCE knowledge area.
bullets: VIS (Vaccine Information Statement): CDC sheet required by federal law before each dose of a covered vaccine. Use the current edition; document the VIS date and the date given.
Give the VIS before immunization — not only afterward and not only if the patient asks.
Post-immunization care: for most vaccines, observe the patient seated or lying down for 15 minutes (most syncope is within 15 minutes).
Some people are observed for 30 minutes after a COVID-19 vaccine.
If the patient feels faint, seat them and notify the pharmacist.
Do not send them to the parking lot untreated.
VAERS = vaccine adverse events. MedWatch = general FDA drug/device/medication-error reports. Know which system matches the product.
OTC recommendation and therapeutic substitution always go to the pharmacist (3.3).
Purple Book (FDA licensed biologics / interchangeability) is not named on the January 2026 outline — skip it as tested content.
Orange Book A/AB remains the small-molecule TE shorthand in Federal notes.

modules.title: Reading Prescriptions & SIG Codes
modules.desc: Prescription components, abbreviations, administration supplies, NDC and expiration, and returns.

lessons.title: Parts of a Prescription
lessons.intro: A prescription has defined parts; understanding them is essential for accurate order entry.
bullets: Inscription: the medication name and strength.
Subscription: the dispensing instructions — quantity to dispense and any special preparation.
Signa ("sig"): the directions for the patient (how to take it).
"Disp #30" = dispense a quantity of 30; refills are authorized separately (e.g., "Refills: 2").
Other elements: prescriber info + DEA number (for controls), patient name/DOB/address, date written, and prescriber signature.
Red flags requiring pharmacist clarification: illegible handwriting, unusual dose, missing quantity/sig, dangerous abbreviations.

lessons.title: Common SIG Codes & Abbreviations
lessons.intro: Recognize the high-frequency abbreviations used in directions. qd and the eye/ear codes are ISMP error-prone: know the meaning, and write the words instead.
bullets: Frequency: qd means daily, but it is error-prone — do not use it; write daily. BID (twice daily), TID (three times), QID (four times), q4h/q6h (every 4/6 hours), qhs (every night at bedtime), PRN (as needed).
Meals/timing: ac (before meals), pc (after meals), hs (at bedtime).
Routes: PO (by mouth), SL (sublingual), PR (rectally), top (topically), IM/IV/SubQ (injections).

Eyes/ears — recognize, do not use: OU = both eyes, OD = right eye, OS = left eye; AU = both ears, AD = right ear, AS = left ear. Write both eyes, right eye, left eye, both ears, right ear, or left ear.
Amounts: i = one, ii = two, ss = one-half; tab = tablet, cap = capsule, gtt(s) = drop(s), supp = suppository.
Other: ud / ut dict = as directed, STAT = immediately, NR = no refills, DAW = dispense as written.
keyPoints: qhs = at bedtime; qh = every hour
OU/OD/OS and AU/AD/AS: recognize; write the eye or ear

lessons.title: Administration Supplies
lessons.intro: Match the measuring device, diluent, and vaccine needle to the product label.
bullets: Oral solutions (Dilaudid label): measure with a graduated oral syringe or measuring cup in mL, not a household teaspoon or tablespoon.
U-100 insulin syringe: Humulin N labeling says doses are measured in units, U-100 insulin contains 100 units/mL (1 mL = 1 cc), and the syringe must be marked for U-100 insulin.
Spacer: FLOVENT HFA labeling says a valved holding chamber (a kind of spacer) and face mask may be used to deliver FLOVENT HFA to young patients.
Dry-powder inhaler: do not use PROAIR RESPICLICK with a spacer or volume holding chamber.
Nebulizer: a device that sprays liquids in aerosol form into gases delivered directly to the patient for breathing. Heated, ultrasonic, gas, venturi, and refillable nebulizers are included. Class II.
Sterile Water for Injection: a diluent for parenteral drugs. Do not inject it until it is made approximately isotonic. Not for direct infusion.
Bacteriostatic Water for Injection contains 0.9% (9 mg/mL) or 1.1% (11 mg/mL) benzyl alcohol. For neonates, use only preservative-free Sterile Water for Injection.
Label-directed diluent: dilute Humalog U-100 to 0.1 unit/mL–1.0 unit/mL with 0.9% sodium chloride.
Adult IM vaccine supplies (CDC): 1 mL or 3 mL syringe, 22- to 25-gauge needle, 1- to 1.5-inch needle, inserted at 90 degrees.
Subcutaneous vaccine needle (CDC): 23- to 25-gauge, 5/8 inch (16 mm), inserted at 45 degrees.
keyPoints: Oral liquid: mL syringe, not a household spoon
Match the device on the label: oral mL syringe, U-100 syringe, spacer only if the inhaler allows it

lessons.title: NDC, Lot, and Expiration
lessons.intro: The package carries an NDC, a lot number, and an expiration date.
bullets: FDA 10-digit NDC: labeler (assigned by FDA) – product (strength, dosage form, and formulation) – package (size and type). Configurations: 4-4-2, 5-3-2, or 5-4-1. A padded 12345-0678-09 can be 12345-678-09 or 12345-0678-9.
On March 7, 2033, FDA-assigned NDCs convert to 12-digit 6-4-2 (6-digit labeler, 4-digit product, 2-digit package) by adding leading zeros to the short segments.
That rule does not change the HIPAA 11-digit format used for reimbursement. FDA does not intend to object to 10-digit NDCs on labels from March 7, 2033 through March 6, 2036.
Lot number: it should yield the complete manufacturing history of the package. An incorrect lot number may misbrand the article.
Expiration date: once it has passed there is no guarantee the medicine will be safe and effective. If it has expired, do not use it.

Expiration dating follows the storage conditions on the label. If the product is reconstituted at dispensing, the label bears expiration information for both the reconstituted and unreconstituted products.

The expiration date appears on the immediate container and the outer package, unless it is easily legible through the outer package. Single-dose containers in individual cartons may show the date on the carton instead.
keyPoints: Lot = manufacturing history; do not use after expiration

lessons.title: Returns
lessons.intro: Credit returns, non-creditable hazardous waste, and reverse distribution are different paths.
bullets: Credit return: a potentially creditable hazardous waste pharmaceutical is a prescription hazardous waste pharmaceutical expected to receive manufacturer credit, in the original manufacturer packaging (except a recall), undispensed, and unexpired or less than one year past expiration. A reverse distributor receives it to verify that credit.

Non-creditable hazardous waste pharmaceutical: no reasonable expectation of manufacturer credit. Includes investigational drugs, free samples, residues in empty containers, and spill-cleanup material.

Reverse distribute (controlled substances): a DEA-registered reverse distributor acquires them from another registrant or law enforcement to return them to the registered manufacturer, or to a registrant the manufacturer authorizes, or for destruction.
A reverse distributor destroys a controlled substance received for destruction no later than 30 calendar days after receipt.

Returned drug product is identified and held. If storage, shipping, or the container casts doubt on safety, identity, strength, quality, or purity, it is destroyed unless testing proves those standards. Records include lot number, reason, quantity, and disposition.
keyPoints: Credit return: original pack, undispensed, unexpired or <1 year past expiration

modules.title: Pharmacy Calculations
modules.desc: Conversions, days supply, ratio/percent strength, dilution, and IV flow rates. Alligation is not a 2026 tested skill.

lessons.title: Conversions & Household Measures
lessons.intro: Master the unit conversions that underpin most calculation questions.
bullets: Weight: 1 kg = 2.2 lb. Convert lb→kg by dividing by 2.2 (154 lb ÷ 2.2 = 70 kg).
Volume: 1 tsp = 5 mL; 1 tbsp = 15 mL = 3 tsp; 1 fl oz ≈ 30 mL; 1 L = 1000 mL.
Weight (metric): 1 g = 1000 mg; 1 mg = 1000 mcg.
Apothecary: 1 grain (gr) ≈ 65 mg (often rounded to 60 mg).
Roman numerals: ss = ½, I = 1, V = 5, X = 10, L = 50, C = 100, D = 500, M = 1000. (XLIV = 44, XC = 90.)

lessons.title: Dosage, Days Supply & Quantity
lessons.intro: The most common calculation tasks: dose size, days supply, and quantity to dispense.
bullets: Dose from strength: (desired dose ÷ available strength) × quantity per unit. 250 mg needed, 125 mg tabs → 2 tabs.
Proportion: a/b = c/d, so a×d = b×c. 250 mg/5 mL = x/20 mL → x = (250×20)÷5 = 1,000 mg.
Weight-based dose: mg/kg/day × weight in kg (15 mg/kg/day × 18 kg = 270 mg/day).
Days supply (tablets): quantity ÷ tablets per day. 90 tabs at TID (3/day) = 30 days. Round DOWN for billing.
Insulin days supply: (mL × 100 units for U-100) ÷ units per day. A 10 mL vial = 1,000 units; at 20 units/day lasts 50 days.
Eye/ear drops: total drops = mL × 20 drops/mL; days = total drops ÷ drops per day. 30 mL at 4 drops/day = 150 days.
Inhalers: days = total actuations ÷ puffs per day. 200 actuations at 2 puffs BID (4/day) = 50 days.

lessons.title: Ratio/Percent Strength & Dilution
lessons.intro: Concentration expressions and dilution still appear on the PTCE (outline 4.1). Alligation was removed from the January 2026 calculation list — it lives in the optional archive lesson that follows.
bullets: Percent w/v (solutions) = grams per 100 mL. 0.9% NaCl = 0.9 g per 100 mL; in 500 mL that is 4.5 g. D5W = 5 g dextrose per 100 mL (50 g per 1,000 mL).
Percent v/v = mL per 100 mL. Isopropyl alcohol 70% v/v = 70 mL per 100 mL; in 250 mL that is 175 mL.
Ratio strength: 1:1000 = 1 g per 1000 mL = 1 mg/mL (epinephrine).
Percent ↔ decimal: divide by 100 (0.75% = 0.0075). Percent w/w (creams) = grams per 100 g. 1% hydrocortisone cream = 10 mg/g, so 0.25% cream = 2.5 mg/g (% × 10).
Dilution: C1V1 = C2V2 keeps the amount of drug constant when changing concentration/volume — this remains in scope.
keyPoints: w/v = g/100 mL; w/w = g/100 g

lessons.title: IV Flow Rates
lessons.intro: Flow-rate calculations determine how fast an IV runs.
bullets: mL per hour = total volume ÷ total hours. 1,000 mL over 8 hours = 125 mL/hr.
Drops per minute: gtt/min = (volume in mL ÷ time in minutes) × drop factor (gtt/mL).
Example: 1,000 mL over 6 hours with a 15 gtt/mL set → (1000 ÷ 360) × 15 ≈ 42 gtt/min.
Know common drop factors: 10, 15, 20 gtt/mL (macro) and 60 gtt/mL (micro).

lessons.title: Alligation (optional archive)
lessons.intro: OPTIONAL / NOT EMPHASIZED ON THE 2026 PTCE. Alligation was removed from the January 2026 calculation list. Skip it on the default path. Use C1V1 = C2V2 for dilution and concentration.
bullets: Historical method: parts of the higher strength = target − lower; parts of the lower strength = higher − target.
Example (archive only): mix 70% and 20% to make 50% → 30 parts of 70% and 20 parts of 20% = 3:2.
Default 2026 skill: C1V1 = C2V2, percent w/v (g/100 mL) and w/w (g/100 g), and ratio strength (1:1000 = 1 mg/mL).
q136 in the bank is tagged featured:false so it does not enter default exams or weak-area weighting.

modules.title: Insurance Billing & Order Processing
modules.desc: Third-party billing, DAW codes, prior authorization, and coordination of benefits. Not a 2026 PTCE knowledge area — optional archive. The corrected facts stay here for review.

lessons.title: Third-Party Billing & DAW Codes (optional archive)
lessons.intro: OPTIONAL / NOT EMPHASIZED ON THE 2026 PTCE. DAW codes and third-party billing are recommended practice, not a PTCE knowledge area. Skip this lesson on the default path.
bullets: DAW codes: DAW 0 = no product selection indicated (default); DAW 1 = substitution not allowed by prescriber; DAW 2 = substitution allowed, patient requested the brand.
Common rejections: "Refill too soon," "NDC not covered," "Prior authorization required," and incorrect days supply or patient DOB.
Patient identity: full name + date of birth are required to match the correct profile; a DOB mismatch is a common rejection cause.
BIN, PCN, Group, and Member ID numbers on the insurance card route the claim to the correct payer.
keyPoints: DAW 0 = no product selection; DAW 1 = prescriber blocks substitution

lessons.title: Prior Authorization & Coordination of Benefits (optional archive)
lessons.intro: OPTIONAL / NOT EMPHASIZED ON THE 2026 PTCE. Prior authorization and coordination of benefits are recommended practice, not a PTCE knowledge area. Skip this lesson on the default path.
bullets: Prior authorization (PA): the prescriber must justify medical necessity to the insurer BEFORE the claim will pay.
Coordination of benefits (COB) determines which plan is primary when a patient has multiple insurers.
Birthday rule (dependent children on both parents' plans): the primary plan is the parent whose birth MONTH/DAY falls earlier in the calendar year.

For a patient 65 or older covered through current employment (the patient's or a spouse's), the group health plan is primary and Medicare is secondary when the employer has 20 or more employees. Medicare is primary if that employer has fewer than 20 employees, or if there is no current-employment group plan. Medicaid is generally the payer of last resort.

A cash discount card lowers the cash price and is not billed with insurance on that fill. A manufacturer copay coupon is used with commercial insurance to reduce the copay, and must not be used for Medicare or Medicaid.
keyPoints: PA = prescriber justifies to payer first
Age 65, employer 20+: group plan primary, Medicare secondary
Cash discount is not insurance; copay coupon is commercial only

modules.title: Controlled Substances & DEA Regulations
modules.desc: CSA schedules, DEA forms, refill and transfer rules, recordkeeping, and the Combat Methamphetamine Epidemic Act.

lessons.title: Controlled Substance Schedules
lessons.intro: The Controlled Substances Act (1970) created five schedules based on abuse potential and accepted medical use.
bullets: Schedule I: HIGH abuse potential, NO accepted medical use — heroin, LSD, and marijuana that is neither an FDA-approved product nor covered by a state medical-marijuana license. No prescriptions.

Marijuana split (current as of April 28, 2026): FDA-approved marijuana products and marijuana under a qualifying state medical-marijuana license are Schedule III. Other marijuana stays Schedule I while broader rescheduling is still pending. Older materials that list all marijuana as C-I are out of date.
Schedule II: high abuse potential WITH accepted medical use — oxycodone, hydrocodone/APAP (Norco), morphine, fentanyl, amphetamine (Adderall), methylphenidate (Ritalin).
Schedule III: moderate abuse potential — Tylenol #3 (codeine/APAP), buprenorphine products, anabolic steroids.
Schedule IV: lower abuse potential — benzodiazepines (alprazolam, lorazepam), zolpidem (Ambien), tramadol.
Schedule V: lowest abuse potential — some cough preparations with limited codeine (e.g., guaifenesin/codeine), pregabalin (Lyrica).
Buprenorphine is Schedule III. The DATA 2000 X-waiver was eliminated in December 2022 (MAT Act) — a separate X number is no longer required to prescribe buprenorphine for OUD.
keyPoints: FDA-approved and state-licensed medical marijuana = C-III
C-II examples include opioids and stimulants

lessons.title: Schedule II–V Prescription & Refill Rules
lessons.intro: Refill, transfer, and transmission rules differ by schedule.
bullets: C-II: NO refills — a new prescription is required each time; written or electronic (EPCS); no telephone call-ins except a true emergency.

An individual practitioner may issue multiple C-II prescriptions that together total up to a 90-day supply. On each prescription other than the first, if that first one is to be filled immediately, the practitioner writes the earliest date a pharmacy may fill it.

A controlled-substance prescription is dated and signed on the day it is issued. It must show the patient's full name and address, the drug name, strength, dosage form, quantity prescribed, directions for use, and the practitioner's name, address, and registration number.

C-II fax is the original prescription only in three cases: any C-II for a long-term care facility resident; a C-II narcotic for a patient in a qualifying hospice, with hospice noted on the prescription; a C-II narcotic compounded for direct parenteral, IV, IM, subcutaneous, or intraspinal infusion.
C-III and C-IV: up to 5 refills within 6 months of the issue date. Federal law does not set that cap on Schedule V; follow the stricter state rule.

Refills left on a C-III or C-IV: no more than 5 refills, and none after 6 months from the issue date. If 5 were authorized and 2 have been dispensed, 3 remain, and only while the 6-month date has not passed.
Emergency C-II oral authorization: the pharmacist may fill a quantity for the emergency period; the prescriber must deliver a written follow-up prescription within 7 days.

The pharmacist writes the oral order down immediately. Within 7 days the prescriber must deliver a follow-up for that emergency quantity. On paper, the face must read "Authorization for Emergency Dispensing" and the date of the oral order. It may be delivered in person or by mail postmarked within those 7 days, and the pharmacist attaches it to the written oral order. For an electronic prescription, the pharmacist annotates the record with the original authorization and the date of the oral order. If the prescriber fails to deliver the written prescription, the pharmacist notifies the nearest DEA office.

C-II partial fills — if the patient or prescriber requests a partial (CARA 2016), remaining portions must be filled within 30 days of the written date, except an emergency oral C-II, whose remaining portions must be filled within 72 hours after the prescription is issued.
If the pharmacy cannot supply the full C-II quantity, the older rule still applies: remainder within 72 hours, then a new prescription is required.

If that remainder is not or cannot be filled within 72 hours of the first partial, the pharmacist notifies the prescriber. No further quantity may be supplied after those 72 hours without a new prescription.
LTCF or terminally ill patients: remaining portions of C-II partial fills may be dispensed for up to 60 days from the written date.
After the applicable window, leftover quantity cannot be filled. Total dispensed cannot exceed the written amount. Document each partial.
Quantity left on a C-II partial: add every partial and stop at the written quantity. Example: 90 tablets written, 30 then 20 dispensed, 40 left.
C-III–V transfers: one time to another pharmacy for a refill, unless the pharmacies share a real-time online database — then transfers may continue until the refills are used up.

Electronic controlled prescriptions: an unfilled electronic C-II–V prescription may be transferred once for initial dispensing, pharmacist to pharmacist, at the patient’s request. It stays electronic. Authorized C-III–V refills transfer with it. A paper C-II cannot be transferred.
Non-controlled prescriptions: remaining refills may be transferred as state law allows. Federal law does not impose a one-time cap.
keyPoints: C-III and C-IV = 5 refills / 6 months; C-V follows state law
C-II fax original: LTCF any C-II; hospice C-II narcotic; infusion C-II narcotic
CARA request = 30 days, except emergency oral = 72 hours
C-III–V transfer once, unless shared real-time database
E-Rx C-II–V: one initial-fill transfer; C-III–V refills go with it

lessons.title: DEA Forms, Registration & Recordkeeping
lessons.intro: Specific DEA forms document ordering, theft/loss, destruction, and registration of controlled substances.
bullets: DEA Form 222 (single-sheet paper — not the old triplicate — or electronic CSOS): used to ORDER or TRANSFER Schedule I–II. Destruction/disposal is Form 41, never 222.

The registrant, or a person named in a power of attorney, signs Schedule I and II orders on Form 222 or electronically. The registrant (or a partner or officer) and the attorney-in-fact both sign the power of attorney, two witnesses sign it, and it is kept with the order records.

DEA Form 106: theft or significant loss. Two steps — written notice to the local DEA field office within 1 business day of discovery, then electronic Form 106 within 45 calendar days. Paper Form 106 is not accepted.
DEA Form 41: document DESTRUCTION/disposal of pharmacy-owned controlled substances.
DEA Form 224: pharmacy DEA registration; renew every 3 YEARS.

C-II–IV dispensing labels must state: “Caution: Federal law prohibits the transfer of this drug to any person other than the patient for whom it was prescribed.” Schedule V does not require that federal statement.

Keep controlled-substance records (prescriptions, inventories, Form 222s, and invoices) for at least 2 years. Biennial inventory is every 2 years. An opened container of a C-II needs an exact count. An opened C-III–V container may be estimated unless it holds more than 1,000 tablets or capsules, which requires an exact count.
On receipt of a C-II order, record the date and the quantity received on the pharmacy’s copy of Form 222 (or the CSOS record).
Returns of pharmacy stock to a reverse distributor: C-II on DEA Form 222 (or CSOS); C-III–V on an invoice. Patient-owned leftovers use take-back, not that invoice.

DEA number: 2 letters + 7 digits; the 2nd letter usually matches the registrant's last-name initial. Check-digit verification: add digits 1+3+5; add digits 2+4+6 and multiply by 2; the sum's last digit = the 7th digit.
Take-back (2.3): unused patient-owned CS go to a DEA-authorized collector, mail-back, or National Take Back Day — they are never restocked into dispensable inventory.
C-II storage: locked substantially constructed cabinet, or dispersed among non-controls so they are not obvious theft targets.
keyPoints: 106 = written notice in 1 business day, then electronic form in 45 days
CS records kept 2 years; biennial inventory; C-II exact count
Reverse distributor: C-II on 222, C-III–V on invoice

lessons.title: Combat Methamphetamine Epidemic Act (CMEA)
lessons.intro: CMEA restricts OTC sales of pseudoephedrine and ephedrine to curb methamphetamine production.
bullets: Pseudoephedrine (Sudafed) and ephedrine are kept BEHIND THE COUNTER (not a prescription, but restricted).
Daily sales limit: 3.6 grams of pseudoephedrine base, ephedrine base, or phenylpropanolamine base per purchaser per day.

Base, not the salt. A 30 mg pseudoephedrine HCl tablet contains 24.6 mg of pseudoephedrine base. 146 of those tablets are 3.5916 g of base, under the 3.6 g daily limit. 366 of those tablets equal the 9.0 g 30-day purchase limit.
30-day purchase cap: 9 grams of the base per purchaser, of which not more than 7.5 grams of the base may be mail-order.
Requirements: photo ID and a written or electronic logbook (purchaser name, address, and signature; date and time; product; quantity), except one sales package of not more than 60 mg pseudoephedrine.
Products must be stored behind the counter or in a locked cabinet.
keyPoints: 3.6 g base/day; 9 g base/30 days (≤7.5 g mail-order)
Photo ID + logbook (name, address, signature); 60 mg PSE package exception

lessons.title: Restricted Programs: REMS, iPLEDGE & CMEA (2.4)
lessons.intro: Knowledge area 2.4 is federal restricted-drug processing: pseudoephedrine (CMEA) and the REMS programs that are still in effect. A technician stops on a REMS reject and notifies the pharmacist.
bullets: REMS (Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy): extra FDA-required steps for drugs with known serious risks — certification, enrollment, labs, or a Medication Guide given with each fill.

Clozapine is not a current pharmacy REMS. FDA removed the Clozapine REMS effective June 13, 2025. Pharmacies do not enroll or confirm an ANC through a REMS before dispensing. Severe neutropenia risk, the boxed warning, and a Medication Guide remain. ANC monitoring stays with the prescriber, per the labeling.

iPLEDGE (isotretinoin): teratogen. Prescriber, certified pharmacy, and patients enroll — both patients who can get pregnant and patients who cannot get pregnant. Maximum 30-day supply, no refills, authorization before each dispense.

iPLEDGE pickup rule that is current: patients who can get pregnant have a 7-day window counted from pregnancy-test specimen collection. The old 19-day lockout is not current — if that window is missed, a repeat pregnancy test may be done immediately, with no extra waiting period.

TIRF is not a routine current enroll-and-dispense REMS. Production of TIRF medicines stopped September 30, 2024, and the REMS accepts no new patient, prescriber, or pharmacy enrollments. It remains only while the applications stay approved and any remaining supply is dispensed to already enrolled patients. The products were transmucosal immediate-release fentanyl for opioid-tolerant patients.
THALOMID (thalidomide) and REVLIMID (lenalidomide): pregnancy-prevention REMS. Treat them as current restricted programs, not clozapine.
Tech action on any REMS reject: stop, do not override, notify the pharmacist. A paper waiver does not replace REMS.

CMEA sits in the same 2.4 bucket: 3.6 g of base per day (pseudoephedrine, ephedrine, or phenylpropanolamine); 9 g of base per 30 days, of which not more than 7.5 g of base may be mail-order; photo ID + logbook; behind the counter.
keyPoints: iPLEDGE: patients who can get pregnant; no 19-day lockout
Current REMS examples: iPLEDGE, THALOMID/lenalidomide; TIRF is not a new-enrollment REMS
CMEA = 3.6 g base/day; 9 g base/30 days (≤7.5 g mail-order)

modules.title: Patient Privacy, Counseling & Consumer Protection Laws
modules.desc: HIPAA, OBRA-90, and the consumer-protection statutes that shape pharmacy practice.

lessons.title: HIPAA & Patient Privacy (optional archive)
lessons.intro: OPTIONAL / NOT EMPHASIZED ON THE 2026 PTCE. HIPAA protects patients' health information and gives them specific rights. Skip this lesson on the default path.
bullets: HIPAA safeguards Protected Health Information (PHI) — any individually identifiable health information.
Pharmacies must provide a Notice of Privacy Practices (NPP) explaining how PHI is used and disclosed.
Minimum necessary applies to most uses and disclosures. It does not apply to a disclosure to, or a request by, a health care provider for treatment.
PHI may be shared without authorization for Treatment, Payment, and healthcare Operations (TPO).
Avoid discussing patient information in public areas; verify identity before releasing information; shred PHI documents.

lessons.title: OBRA-90 & Counseling Requirements (optional archive)
lessons.intro: OPTIONAL / NOT EMPHASIZED ON THE 2026 PTCE. The Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1990 established counseling and DUR requirements. Skip this lesson on the default path.
bullets: OBRA-90 mandates a prospective drug utilization review (DUR) before dispensing Medicaid prescriptions.

For each Medicaid beneficiary or caregiver who presents a prescription, the pharmacist offers to counsel on matters the pharmacist judges significant. The offer is not limited to new prescriptions. The patient may decline. Where state law is broader, follow the stricter rule.
Counseling content: drug name, purpose, how to take, side effects, storage, and what to do about a missed dose.
Technicians facilitate counseling offers but the pharmacist provides the clinical counseling.
keyPoints: OBRA-90 = Medicaid DUR + offer to counsel (not only new Rx)

lessons.title: Consumer Protection & Packaging Laws
lessons.intro: Several federal laws govern drug safety, labeling, and packaging.
bullets: Pure Food and Drug Act (1906): prohibited adulterated/misbranded drugs — the start of federal drug regulation.
Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FDCA) 1938: required drugs be proven SAFE (after the sulfanilamide elixir disaster); created the FDA's modern authority.
Durham-Humphrey Amendment (1951): established the prescription (legend) vs OTC distinction.
Kefauver-Harris Amendment (1962): required drugs be proven safe AND EFFECTIVE, and established Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP).
Poison Prevention Packaging Act (1970): child-resistant containers for most prescriptions and many OTC drugs. The CPSC enforces it, not the FDA. Sublingual nitroglycerin is exempt.

Non-child-resistant request: a prescriber may request it for one prescription only. The patient may request it, and only the patient may make a blanket request covering all of that patient’s prescriptions. Document the request.
ADA packaging accommodations: easy-off caps, large-print labels, talking labels, and Braille labels.
Medication Guides: when FDA requires one for a drug, give that guide with every fill, including refills — not only the first fill. Some REMS programs include this step.
Drug Listing Act / NDC: every drug has a National Drug Code identifying labeler, product, and package size.
keyPoints: Only the patient may blanket-request non-CRC
Medication Guide with each required fill

modules.title: Agencies, Recalls & Practice Regulations
modules.desc: Regulatory agencies, FDA medication recalls (2.5), hazardous and non-hazardous pharmaceutical waste (2.1), DSCSA product tracing (2.6), and workplace practice rules.

lessons.title: Regulatory Agencies & Their Roles (optional archive)
lessons.intro: OPTIONAL / NOT EMPHASIZED ON THE 2026 PTCE. Know which agency does what — a common exam distinction. Skip this lesson on the default path.
bullets: FDA: drug safety, approval, labeling, recalls, MedWatch, and REMS programs.
DEA: enforces the Controlled Substances Act; registration, schedules, and diversion control.
State Boards of Pharmacy: license pharmacists/technicians and regulate practice within the state.
OSHA: workplace safety — hazardous chemicals, bloodborne pathogens, Safety Data Sheets (SDS).
CDC: immunization guidance and public-health recommendations (with ACIP for vaccines).
NIOSH: identifies hazardous drugs and safe-handling guidance.

lessons.title: Recalls, Expiration & Stock Management
lessons.intro: Outline 2.5 is FDA requirements for medication recalls. Handling recalled and expired stock protects patients. Take-back is a separate 2.3 workflow for patient-owned leftovers.
bullets: Recall classes: Class I = reasonable probability of serious adverse health consequences or death; Class II = temporary or medically reversible harm, or a remote probability of serious harm; Class III = adverse health consequences not likely.

Recall depth is how far the notice goes: wholesale, retail, or consumer (patient) level. A Class I medication recall usually reaches the consumer level, and patients who received the affected lot are notified.
On a recall: identify affected lot numbers, quarantine the stock, and follow manufacturer/wholesaler return instructions.
Rotate stock using FEFO (First-Expired, First-Out) to minimize expired product.
Never dispense expired medication; remove expired/damaged units from active stock promptly.
The NDC number (labeler-product-package) is used to identify recalled products and process returns.
The firm initiates a recall. FDA may request one. Pharmacy action is the same: pull matching lots, quarantine, document, follow the notice.
A market withdrawal is not a recall — the firm removes product for a minor violation that would not usually trigger legal recall action.

A stock recovery is also not a recall. The firm removes or corrects product that has not been marketed or has not left the firm's direct control, and no portion of the lot has been released for sale or use.
Do not confuse a lot-specific recall with a patient take-back of leftover pills from home.
keyPoints: Class I = most serious; usually consumer level + patient notice
Match NDC + lot + expiry, then quarantine

lessons.title: Technician Scope of Practice & Workplace Safety (optional archive)
lessons.intro: OPTIONAL / NOT EMPHASIZED ON THE 2026 PTCE. Technicians work under pharmacist supervision within defined legal boundaries. Skip this lesson on the default path.
bullets: Technicians may: enter orders, fill/count medications, manage inventory, process insurance, and compound under supervision.
Technicians may NOT: provide clinical counseling, perform the final DUR/clinical verification, or take new verbal prescriptions (varies by state).
The pharmacist is responsible for the final check and all clinical decisions.
When a federal rule and a state rule differ, follow the stricter requirement.
Safety Data Sheets (SDS) describe chemical hazards; OSHA requires they be accessible to staff.
State laws and Boards of Pharmacy set technician registration/licensure and ratio requirements.
keyPoints: Stricter of federal or state law applies

lessons.title: DSCSA Essentials for Technicians
lessons.intro: DSCSA (knowledge area 2.6, added on the January 6, 2026 outline) is the federal track-and-trace law for prescription drugs. Learn durable duties — serialization, authorized partners, suspect vs illegitimate handling, and 6-year records — not rapidly changing exemption end-dates.
bullets: Product identifier: each package carries a unique serialized ID (usually a 2D data matrix) with NDC, serial number, lot number, and expiration date.

Current electronic exchange is Transaction Information (TI: product, lot, dates, and the parties) plus a Transaction Statement (TS: the seller attests it is authorized and did not knowingly ship suspect or illegitimate product). Transaction History (TH) was retired in November 2023. Do not memorize a mandatory TI + TH + TS set as current law.
Authorized trading partners: licensed/registered manufacturers, wholesale distributors, dispensers (pharmacies), and repackagers. Accept product only from authorized partners.

Suspect product: reason to believe it may be counterfeit, diverted, stolen, intentionally adulterated, or unfit. Do not dispense. Quarantine it, notify the pharmacist, and verify the product identifier (NDC, serial number, lot, and expiration).

Illegitimate product: credible evidence that it is counterfeit, diverted, stolen, intentionally adulterated, or unfit. Within 24 hours of that determination, notify FDA (Form FDA 3911) and immediate trading partners. Keep DSCSA transaction records for 6 years (not the 2-year CSA clock).
FDA used phased implementation milestones for electronic package-level tracing. Exam focus is the technician duties above, not a specific exemption sunset date.
keyPoints: TI + TS current; TH retired Nov 2023
Suspect: quarantine and verify the identifier

lessons.title: Hazardous & Non-Hazardous Pharmaceutical Waste (2.1)
lessons.intro: Knowledge area 2.1 is federal storage, handling, and disposal of non-hazardous and hazardous pharmaceutical waste, including EPA P-list waste, plus the OSHA exposure steps tested with it.
bullets: EPA RCRA listed waste: P-list drugs are acutely hazardous when the listed chemical is the sole active ingredient. Examples: warfarin above 0.3% (P001); nicotine (P075), except FDA-approved OTC nicotine replacement products, which were removed from that listing. U-list drugs are toxic but not acute. Examples: cyclophosphamide (U058); lindane (U129).

P- and U-lists cover unused discarded commercial chemical products (the pure or technical grade, or a formulation in which the chemical is the sole active ingredient), off-specification product, container residue, and spill residue. That residue is hazardous waste unless the container is empty. A stock bottle, dispensing bottle, vial, or ampule (not over 1 liter or 10,000 pills), or a unit-dose container, is empty once the drug is removed the usual way. A hazardous-waste pharmaceutical that is also a scheduled controlled substance is not sewered. It is collected, stored, transported, and disposed of under DEA rules, and destroyed by a method DEA has publicly deemed non-retrievable or combusted at a permitted facility listed in the EPA rule.

A discarded drug can still be hazardous by characteristic (ignitable, corrosive, reactive, or toxic) when it is not on the P- or U-list. Non-hazardous pharmaceutical waste is the remaining drug waste. “Not on the P-list” does not mean trash or the drain.
The 2019 EPA hazardous-waste pharmaceuticals rule banned sewering hazardous-waste drugs nationwide. Do not flush them.

Segregate waste before it leaves the pharmacy. The color map commonly used on the PTCE: black = RCRA hazardous pharmaceutical waste; yellow = trace chemotherapy; red = biohazard, including sharps; blue or white = non-hazardous pharmaceutical waste. Follow the pharmacy’s waste-vendor labels when they differ — the federal duty is segregation, not one national color statute.

OSHA bloodborne pathogens: never recap a used needle by hand. Discard sharps at once in a rigid, puncture-resistant, closable container. After a needle-stick, wash the site, report it immediately, and follow post-exposure evaluation and prophylaxis (PEP).

OSHA exposure controls: know where the eyewash and the spill kit are. Flush eyes at the eyewash — 15 minutes is the usual tested minimum — and follow the Safety Data Sheet. Right-to-know (Hazard Communication): staff must be able to reach the SDS for hazardous chemicals they handle.
keyPoints: Black = RCRA hazardous; yellow = trace chemo
Eyewash, spill kit, and SDS access
